name: Dana Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, with a master’s degree, and I lead batch-label software for a food-manufacturing tech company. I am good at tracing where a lot number went wrong, but I do not use AI tools and still want another engineer to read a critical change. Iris runs a small bookshop; we have two school-age children, a mortgage and about ten months saved, and I like a release that can be explained from the factory log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our team that a small AI tool may tidy routine reports, but a food batch still needs the right lot number before it leaves the factory. I do not use AI tools; I check the code and the factory record with another engineer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a master’s degree, strong skills and high pay for a lead developer, with around ten months of expenses saved. My partner Iris runs a small bookshop; with two children and a mortgage, we can cover bills even when shop sales wobble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing batch-label code and ask the factory desk for one mismatch report each week. We would keep saving 320 monthly from my wage if it holds, rather than renovate a kitchen that still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about this picture. The bookshop has uneven weeks, but our buffer absorbs them and my work stays needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a wrong lot number look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A box of biscuits carried a number from the previous day, and the factory almost sent it out. I compared the printed label with the production log before the batch was released.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why refuse the small AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can explain each check I write and where the evidence came from. I do not want an answer I cannot trace when a food recall starts.

say: I want **lot numbers** checked against the factory record.
I explain **my code checks** to another engineer before release.
think: I have **ten months saved** and higher-than-usual lead pay.
I see our **mortgage covered** even when bookshop sales wobble.
do: **Keep reviewing** batch-label code and weekly mismatch reports.
**Save 320 monthly** while my wage holds; delay kitchen renovation.
feel: **Calm** about secure work and a strong buffer.
S0.quote: I do not want an answer I cannot trace when a food recall starts.
fieldNote: Her refusal of AI comes from **traceable evidence**, not lack of computer skill.
High pay and **ten months saved** buffer uneven bookshop sales while the household continues to pay a mortgage.

steps.text: Keep reviewing batch-label code and weekly factory mismatch reports
Save 320 monthly while lead-developer pay holds
Delay renovating the kitchen while it still works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking checking, buying and coding will change the batch system, but someone must still sign a release with a real name. I would ask management to publish how many developers and factory reviewers remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine label checks my team handles could go first, then management may ask fewer engineers to own all the exceptions. I think my own role could shrink if the firm wants one lead over several factories, though ten months saved gives us a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the director this month for a written staffing plan and keep a log of which batch errors still need people. In the first year I’d observe a colleague testing AI on fake lot numbers during paid time if allowed, but I would not run the tool myself yet; I’d check paid quality-software lead openings if our team starts cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my role, not impressed by a fast report. A factory mistake can follow a family home in a packet of food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why watch but not use the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my colleague can show a genuine mismatch it catches, I might change my mind later. Watching one demonstration does not mean I can run it safely myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Iris?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner Iris we should postpone the kitchen work until the company shows us the staffing plan. Her shop can cover its own rent, but I would not ask it to replace my salary.

say: I want **named sign-off** when AI writes batch checks.
I want **staffing numbers** for developers and factory reviewers.
think: I expect **routine checks** to leave my team first.
I fear **my lead role** could shrink across factories despite savings.
do: **Request staffing plan** and log errors requiring human checks.
**Watch AI demonstration** on fake lots during allowed paid time; postpone kitchen work until the written staffing plan.
**Check paid quality-software openings** if our team starts cutting.
feel: **Anxious** about my own lead role and factory accountability.
S1.quote: A factory mistake can follow a family home in a packet of food.
fieldNote: She **watches AI** but does not use it, so no learn-ai tag is claimed.
Her strong cushion lets her **delay renovation** while seeking facts about staffing.

steps.text: Observe paid AI demonstration on fake lots; await staffing plan before changing current work

Postpone kitchen renovation until company provides written staffing plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write our code and check factory records as well as people. Robots for hands-on packing and bookshop work may arrive around 2031, so both those jobs change later than my desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead job could end even if I have been careful for years. Ten months saved is a proper runway, but it is not a salary, and I do not know which firms would still need developers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop planning the kitchen renovation and ask the company for written notice of any lead cuts now. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I am displaced, I’d seek paid factory quality roles only where vacancies exist and wages cover our mortgage and basic bills; I would not buy machinery to start a business on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed, but I could think straight. A pantry full of food is not the same as a dependable pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Iris’s bookshop support the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps, but shop sales change with the season and it has its own bills. I would not count last December’s good month as a year of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid factory placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No; I would take a paid role that uses my batch knowledge if one exists. I cannot train myself into a wage by giving away months of work.

say: I say **thinking AGI in 2028** reaches code and factory records first.
I know **packing robots around 2031** follow later.
think: I expect my **lead developer job** could end despite experience.
I know **ten months saved** gives search time, not a wage.
do: **Pause kitchen renovation** and request written lead-cut notice now.
**Seek paid factory quality** only if displaced after 2028 and vacancies cover bills.
feel: **Alarmed but clear-headed** about losing a salary.
S2.quote: A pantry full of food is not the same as a dependable pay slip.
fieldNote: Her **2028 desk-work loss** comes before packing and retail robots, leaving the bookshop as an uncertain second wage.
She rejects **unfunded machinery** and a free placement despite strong savings.

steps.text: Pause kitchen renovation instead of spending the household buffer
Seek paid factory-quality vacancies if displaced after 2028 and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 gives us time to find out which food-safety decisions people still have to own. Robots for physical packing and bookshop work may follow around 2034, but the code changes earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn more about recall decisions while still earning my lead wage, though AGI might also reason through them. We could save a full year of bills if my pay and Iris’s shop income hold, but I would not call a recall office safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the factory quality lead for two anonymized label-mismatch cases monthly and decide how I would handle them, only if her employer and mine approve paid time. We’d save 280 monthly if both incomes hold; after 2031 I’d apply for paid quality-review openings only if my developer role ends and the vacancies pay enough for our mortgage and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious but better able to plan. Five years lets me test whether I can explain a recall without pretending the work is permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you decide in a case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare the production log, the printed box and the date a customer could have bought it. I would ask the quality lead which part of my answer she disagreed with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refuses access?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my software job and read public recall reports on my own time. I would not claim that an unapproved visit taught me the factory role.

I know **packing robots around 2034** follow later.
think: I could learn **recall decisions** while earning my current wage.
I might build **a year of bills** if wages and shop income hold.
do: **Decide two mismatch cases** monthly only with both employers approving paid time; otherwise read public recall reports while employed.
**Save 280 monthly** while both household incomes hold.
**Apply for quality review** only if displaced after 2031 and vacancies cover bills.
feel: **Anxious but prepared** with time for approved real cases.
S3.quote: I would not claim that an unapproved visit taught me the factory role.
fieldNote: Her learning requires **two employers’ approval** and paid access to anonymized cases.
The **year-of-bills goal** depends on both incomes continuing and does not make a paid recall office certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 gives firms time to make food records clearer and families time to reduce mortgage debt. Robots for packing and retail may follow around 2039, after our code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older, but I will not count on them to pay our mortgage. I could build eighteen months of bills if both incomes last, while accepting that even recall checking may be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the batch team and keep one anonymized example of a label error and correction each quarter. We’d pay 250 extra monthly toward mortgage principal if both incomes hold; if my developer role ends after 2036, I’d seek paid food-quality work only where vacancies remain and wages cover our bills. We would move only after local search and a written paid offer covering bills, new housing, moving costs and both children’s school travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about a far job change but secure in the next few years. I would rather make the mortgage smaller than make a grand promise about a safe trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the example show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wrong lot number, the production record and who stopped the batch. I could show the chain of evidence without taking a factory customer’s name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a written paid offer covers our bills, a new housing payment, moving costs and both children’s school travel. There are many software firms nearby, so I would search locally first.

I know **packing robots around 2039** follow the code change.
think: I will not rely on **children’s future wages** for the mortgage.
I might build **eighteen months of bills** if both incomes hold.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the code and record checking I lead could end across firms at once. Written notice and a real paid factory-quality vacancy that covers the mortgage would help while we use our savings carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether Iris’s bookshop could fund a year without my wage. A good December at the bookshop cannot replace a steady developer salary.

headlineQuote: A good December at the bookshop cannot replace a steady developer salary.
portrait: Dana is a **43-year-old team lead** with a master’s degree, higher pay and about ten months of expenses saved.
She and Iris support **two children** and a mortgage while bookshop sales vary.
She **never uses AI** and insists on traceable factory records before a batch leaves.
Her **2028 worry** is a lost developer wage; packing and retail robots follow about three years later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her lead software wage before a paid factory role appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a bill-covering paid quality opening and careful use of savings would help.
